```{r, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

In a top-down game, a tree has two jobs: its canopy can hide the hero, while
its trunk blocks movement. A bush works the same way. Use separate objects
for appearance and collision so the player can walk behind the foliage
without walking through its base.

| Part | Purpose | shinyphaser API |
|---|---|---|
| Tree or bush image | Draw the whole object, including foliage | `add_image()`, `set_depth()` |
| Invisible footprint | Block a small area on the ground | `add_collision_rectangle()`, `add_collider()` |
| Hero's feet | Determine where the hero stands | Small Arcade Physics body |
| Depth ordering | Draw the hero behind or in front as it moves | Ground-position depth, updated in the browser |

The complete implementation lives in `inst/examples/swamps_rpg`. With the
current development version installed, run it from the repository root:

```{r eval=FALSE}
shiny::runApp("inst/examples/swamps_rpg")
```

## Draw the image and block only its base

The following snippets use the Swamps RPG resource path registered by that
example. Put the R setup inside its server, after binding `game` to the session
and creating `hero`. For another app, register your own image directory first.

`tree_1.png` is 200 by 400 pixels. Its image is centered, so placing its center
at `base_y - 200` puts the bottom at `base_y`. The depth uses that ground
position, rather than the center of the tall image.

```{r eval=FALSE}
base_x <- 600
base_y <- 1000

tree <- game$add_image(
  "tree", "swamps-rpg-assets/terrain/mushroom_swamps/tree_1.png",
  x = base_x, y = base_y - 400 / 2
)
tree$set_depth(base_y)

# A short, narrow rectangle around the trunk's base, not the entire canopy.
game$add_collision_rectangle(
  "tree_footprint", x = base_x, y = base_y - 12,
  width = 64, height = 24
)
game$add_collider("hero", "tree_footprint")
```

The invisible rectangle has a static physics body. The collider prevents the
hero from crossing it from any direction. The image itself has no physics
body: overlapping the canopy is allowed. Use the same pattern for bushes,
with a footprint sized to the part of the bush that touches the ground.

An object is fully passable if you omit its footprint and collider. Hiding
an image does **not** remove its separate footprint; manage both objects
together when hiding, removing, or switching maps.

## Give the hero a foot-sized collision body

The Orc has 100 by 100 pixel animation frames. Using the entire frame for
collision would prevent the hero from getting close to the foliage. A 32 by
18 pixel body, offset 34 pixels from the frame's left and 72 from its top,
limits collision to the feet.

For this centered sprite, its ground position is `hero.y + 40`: the frame
starts at `hero.y - 50`, and the feet end at pixel 90 within the frame.
These dimensions are specific to this artwork; adjust them for your own hero.

## Change depth as the hero walks

`set_depth()` sets a fixed drawing depth from R. Larger values draw in front.
The scenery stays at `base_y`, but a moving hero needs its depth refreshed
from its current ground position. This needs to happen in the browser each
frame, rather than through a Shiny observer.

The small JavaScript helper below is **app-specific code**, not a new
shinyphaser method. Include it with `tags$script(HTML(...))` in the UI, after
`game$use_phaser()`. It waits for the asynchronously loaded hero by checking
for it on each scene update, then configures the feet once.

```javascript
window.configureObjectDepth = function () {
  const scene = window.game.scene.scenes[0];
  let feetConfigured = false;
  const update = function () {
    const hero = scene.children.getByName("hero");
    if (!hero || !hero.body) return;
    if (!feetConfigured) {
      hero.body.setSize(32, 18);
      hero.body.setOffset(34, 72);
      feetConfigured = true;
    }
    hero.setDepth(hero.y + 40);
  };
  scene.events.on("postupdate", update);
  scene.events.once("shutdown", function () {
    scene.events.off("postupdate", update);
  });
};
```

Install the helper once per scene from the server:

```{r eval=FALSE}
session$sendCustomMessage("phaser", list(js = "configureObjectDepth();"))
```

When the hero's feet are above the tree's base, its depth is smaller, so the
canopy draws over the hero. When its feet are below the base, the hero draws
in front. The footprint blocks movement at the trunk, independently of this
visual ordering. This is often called **Y sorting**.

Keep screen-fixed text and health bars at a depth above the world, for example:

```{r eval=FALSE}
status$set_scroll_factor(0)
status$set_depth(10000)
```

For a 6400-pixel-tall world, 10000 leaves the HUD above all ground-position
depths. In the full example, `www/scenery.js` applies the same ordering to
the hero, enemies, and NPCs, and keeps the HUD above them.

## Place objects only on grass

Swamps RPG reads its Tiled JSON map and identifies tiles whose tileset names
start with `mushroom_swamps_grass_`. Before placing an object, it checks every
tile under the image's full bounding box, not just the trunk. This keeps
both the footprint and the overhanging artwork away from swamp and bank tiles.

The layout generator in `modules/scenery_layout.R` shuffles candidate positions
and places five copies of each tree and fifteen of each bush. It also leaves
space between images and around the hero's spawn, NPCs, enemies, and berries.
A fixed random seed gives every session the same layout, so loading a saved
game does not move the trees or introduce a new obstacle at the saved position.

The rendering module, `modules/scenery.R`, creates each image and its footprint,
sets the image's depth with `set_depth()`, and adds the hero collider. Both
object names are included in the realm's object list so map visibility changes
apply to the artwork and its blocking body together.

To check your own version, walk behind the canopy, walk in front, and approach
the footprint from both sides. The first two should change the drawing order;
the last should stop the hero without blocking the entire visible image.
